text: You've spent six chapters building controls — Conditional Access policies in Chapter 1, an MFA rollout in Chapter 2, a GPO baseline in Chapter 4. This chapter asks a different question: once you know what a control should say, how do you change it safely and visibly, instead of clicking through a portal once and hoping someone remembers why it was set that way? A control is a decision about how the organization is protected, and that decision belongs in a file in a repository, not in a setting only one admin can reconstruct.

A Conditional Access policy or an Azure Policy definition can be written as a Terraform resource instead of portal clicks. Here, azuread_conditional_access_policy defines a policy that requires MFA for admin roles, with its display name, state, and grant controls spelled out as plain text. That block is the policy itself — anyone on the team can read it, diff it against the previous version, and see exactly which role it targets and what it demands, with no tribal knowledge of which blade or checkbox to go find in the portal.

Putting that file in a pull request means a second person reviews the change before it's ever enabled, the same discipline the automation course taught for scripts, now applied to the control itself. In this diff, a reviewer notices Privileged Role Administrator is missing from the targeted roles and asks for it to be added before approving the merge. That question gets answered on a diff, days before the policy goes live — not after an auditor asks why that role was never covered.

On-prem GPO baselines get the same rollback discipline with Backup-GPO and Import-GPO. Backup-GPO saves a point-in-time snapshot of every single setting inside a GPO before you touch it. If a later change breaks something, Import-GPO restores that exact prior snapshot back onto the GPO using its backup ID — a real, verifiable rollback to a known-good state, not an admin trying to recall from memory what the settings used to be before the change went in.

Writing a control down as code doesn't, by itself, prove that control works correctly once it's live. Next: testing a control in audit mode or Conditional Access's report-only mode first, and rolling it out to a small pilot group before it ever applies to the whole organization — simulate first, enforce second.
